chunks: And with this chain, from Ar-Rida (peace be upon him), from his father (peace be upon him from his father (peace be upon him), who said:

As-Sadiq (peace be upon him) saw a man whose grief over his son had become intense, so he said to him: 'O man, are you so grieved over the minor calamity and have you neglected the major calamity? If you had been prepared for when your son would pass away, your grief over him would not have been so intense. Your calamity in leaving yourself unprepared for him is greater than your calamity in the loss of your son.'
ai.seo_question: What is the difference between minor and major calamities in Shia Islamic teachings on grief?
ai.summary: In this tradition from *Uyun Akhbar al-Rida*, Imam As-Sadiq (a.s.) diagnoses the man's grief as a symptom of spiritual negligence rather than mere emotional attachment, highlighting the Shia emphasis on *Tayyib al-Nafs* (purification of the soul) as the true preparation for death. The Imam posits that the 'major calamity' is the failure to cultivate the spiritual readiness required for the transition of the soul, rendering the physical loss secondary to the eternal consequence of being unprepared. This reflects the broader scholarly view that death is not an end but a transition, and one's state at the moment of parting determines their ultimate fate.

en.dr-ali-peiravi: 31-200 According to the same documentation, it is narrated that Ar-Ridha’ (a.s.) quoted on the authority of his father (a.s.),

“Once As-Sadiq (a.s.) saw a man who was seriously upset over the death of his son. The Imam (a.s.) told him, ‘Are you so upset about such a minor calamity and have you forgotten about the major calamity? If you had prepared yourself earlier for the loss of your son you would not have become so upset now. This lack of preparedness for the loss of your son is worse than his actual loss.’”
